introduction: The Earth is surrounded by a massive blanket of gases called the Atmosphere, which is held in place by the planet's gravitational pull. It protects us from harmful solar radiation and regulates temperature. At this beginner level, we will memorize the exact composition of air and the five distinct layers of the atmosphere.

core_concepts.title: Composition of the Atmosphere
core_concepts.description: The air we breathe is a mixture of gases. The most abundant is Nitrogen (78%), followed by Oxygen (21%). The remaining 1% consists of trace gases, with Argon being the third most abundant (0.93%), and Carbon Dioxide making up a tiny but crucial 0.04%.

core_concepts.title: Troposphere (The Weather Layer)
core_concepts.description: This is the lowest layer of the atmosphere (0 to 18 km at the equator, 8 km at the poles). Almost all 'weather phenomena' (clouds, rain, storms) occur exclusively here. In this layer, temperature decreases as altitude increases (this is known as the Normal Lapse Rate: a drop of 1°C for every 165 meters).

core_concepts.title: Stratosphere (The Ozone Layer)
core_concepts.description: Located directly above the troposphere (up to 50 km). It is free from clouds and weather disturbances, making it the ideal layer for flying commercial jet airplanes. Most importantly, it contains the 'Ozone Layer' (O3), which absorbs harmful Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the Sun.

core_concepts.title: Mesosphere, Thermosphere, and Exosphere
core_concepts.description: 1. Mesosphere: The coldest layer where meteors burn up upon entering Earth. 2. Thermosphere: Contains the 'Ionosphere', which reflects radio waves back to Earth (enabling radio communication) and is where Auroras occur. 3. Exosphere: The outermost layer that gradually fades into the vacuum of space.

important_entities.name: Ozone (O3)
important_entities.significance: Without the ozone layer in the Stratosphere, lethal amounts of UV radiation would reach the Earth's surface, destroying DNA and causing massive spikes in skin cancer. Ozone depletion is primarily caused by CFCs (Chlorofluorocarbons) used in old refrigerants.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A classic exam trap: When asked for the third most abundant gas in the atmosphere, students often guess Carbon Dioxide (CO2). This is incorrect. The third most abundant gas is 'Argon' (0.93%). CO2 is fourth (0.04%).

mnemonics_and_tricks.trick_title: Order of the Layers (Bottom to Top)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: T(Troposphere), S(Stratosphere - skipped in acronym for flow, remember it holds the shield), M(Mesosphere), I/T(Ionosphere/Thermosphere), E(Exosphere).

exam_strategy_tips: If an exam asks 'In which layer do commercial airplanes fly?', always select the Stratosphere (or lower stratosphere) because the lack of weather provides a smooth, turbulence-free flight.
Radio wave reflection happens in the 'Ionosphere' (part of the Thermosphere).
